claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion is governed by a dynamic, self-replenishing passive film.
Nanoscale microstructural heterogeneities directly modulate the self-replenishing passive-film mechanism.
Nanoscale heterogeneities promote rapid localized repassivation after mechanical disruption of the passive film.
Rapid localized repassivation produces combined degradation below the additive sum of isolated wear and isolated corrosion.
The proposed initial material is an as-processed AlCoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloy.
The initial AlCoCrFeNi-based alloy contains nanoscale heterogeneities such as grain boundaries or secondary-phase particles.
The initial AlCoCrFeNi-based alloy has a pre-existing passive film.
Matched specimens will be compared under isolated wear, isolated corrosion, and simultaneous wear-corrosion conditions.
Mechanical wear intermittently disrupts the passive film.
Grain boundaries, segregated phases, and secondary particles act as nucleation sites for oxide formation and rapid film repair.
At moderate mechanical loads, rapid repassivation counteracts passive-film loss and reduces net degradation.
If mechanical load or corrosive aggressiveness exceeds the repassivation capacity, the film loses integrity and damage accelerates.
At moderate load and electrolyte aggressiveness, combined degradation will be lower than the arithmetic sum of isolated wear and corrosion.
At high loads or in highly aggressive electrolytes, combined degradation will rise sharply beyond either isolated wear or isolated corrosion.
The beneficial subadditive effect should hold under moderate mechanical and chemical challenges but fail under extreme challenges.
The load and electrolyte-aggressiveness thresholds at which repassivation becomes insufficient are not defined.
EIS, friction and wear measurements, polarization-derived corrosion current, and post-test SEM/EDS will be used to assess film behavior and degradation.
A combined degradation rate equal to the arithmetic sum of isolated wear and corrosion rates would falsify the proposed subadditive mechanism.
